# Sequence searching {#sec-sequence-searching}

::: {.callout-note title="From the exam description"}
Both historical and state-of-the-art methods are used for speed and
accuracy. Understanding the advantages of different algorithms is essential.
:::

## Overview

Finding sequences that are similar to a query is the most frequently used
operation in bioinformatics. It is the first step in annotating a new gene,
building a family alignment, inferring a phylogeny or predicting a
structure. This chapter follows the development of the field:

- what homology is, and how it relates to sequence similarity
  (@sec-ch01-homology);
- exact alignment by dynamic programming and the substitution matrices
  that score it (@sec-ch01-dp);
- the heuristic and indexing methods that make database search fast, and
  the statistics that tell us which hits to trust (@sec-ch01-heuristic);
- comparing sequences without aligning them, by their $k$-mers
  (@sec-ch01-alignfree);
- multiple alignments, motifs, profiles and profile hidden Markov models,
  which capture whole families and find more distant relationships
  (@sec-ch01-profiles);
- how the same ideas are extended to RNA, where structure is conserved
  better than sequence (@sec-ch01-rna);
- protein domains and the databases that classify them
  (@sec-ch01-domains);
- protein language models and how they are starting to be used to detect
  remote homology (@sec-ch01-plm);
- how search methods are benchmarked, and what can go wrong
  (@sec-ch01-benchmarks).

## Key concepts

A checklist for revision. You should be able to explain each point,
including the algorithm or argument behind it, and its limitations.

- **Homology:** definition as common ancestry (qualitative, not a percentage); orthologs, paralogs (in-/out-paralogs), xenologs, ohnologs; analogy and convergence; why significant similarity implies homology but not the reverse; the twilight and midnight zones; why proteins are compared rather than DNA
- **Dynamic programming:** principle of optimality; Needleman–Wunsch and Smith–Waterman recursions and traceback; semi-global, overlap and banded alignment; linear, affine and convex gap penalties; Gotoh's three-matrix algorithm; time and space complexity, Hirschberg/Myers–Miller linear space
- **Substitution matrices:** log-odds scores, target and background frequencies, relative entropy; how PAM and BLOSUM are derived and how their numbering differs; choosing a matrix
- **Heuristic search:** FASTA (k-tuples, diagonals, banded optimisation); BLAST (neighbourhood words, threshold $T$, X-drop, two-hit method, gapped extension); low-complexity filtering; the BLAST family and translated searches; DIAMOND, MMseqs2 and Linclust; Foldseek and the 3Di alphabet
- **Statistics:** why local scores follow a Gumbel distribution; Karlin–Altschul $E = Kmn\,e^{-\lambda S}$; bit scores, E- and P-values; effective lengths, gapped and composition-based statistics; why E-values depend on database size
- **Exact matching:** suffix trees and arrays; the Burrows–Wheeler transform, LF mapping, FM-index and backward search; why they suit read mapping
- **Multiple alignment:** sum-of-pairs score and NP-hardness; progressive alignment and "once a gap, always a gap"; ClustalW, Clustal Omega, T-Coffee (consistency), MUSCLE and MAFFT (iterative refinement); benchmarks
- **Motifs and profiles:** consensus, PROSITE patterns, PWMs with pseudocounts, information content and logos; Gibbs sampling and MEME; Gribskov profiles; sequence weighting and priors; PSI-BLAST and profile corruption
- **Hidden Markov models:** states, transitions, emissions; Viterbi, forward, backward, posterior decoding and Baum–Welch; profile HMM architecture (match/insert/delete, Plan 7), local and glocal modes; HMMER3 filter pipeline and forward-score E-values; HHsearch/HHblits (HMM–HMM comparison); sequence–sequence < sequence–profile < profile–profile
- **Domains:** structural, folding and evolutionary definitions; multidomain proteins and architectures; why domains complicate annotation transfer; Pfam (seed/full alignments, gathering thresholds, clans), Pfam-N, InterPro; SCOP, CATH, ECOD and TED, and fold vs. superfamily
- **RNA homology search:** why RNA homologues share structure rather than sequence; compensatory mutations and covariation; Nussinov and Zuker folding algorithms; SCFGs and their relation to HMMs (CYK, inside–outside); covariance models, Infernal and its HMM filters; Rfam; limitations (pseudoknots, unstructured ncRNAs)
- **Alignment-free comparison:** $k$-mer statistics; MinHash and the Mash distance; ANI and Kraken; when alignment-free methods work and when they fail
- **Protein language models:** masked and autoregressive objectives; transformers and attention; UniRep, SeqVec, ESM, ProtTrans, ESMFold, ESM3; per-residue and per-protein embeddings; embedding search, TM-Vec, pLM-BLAST, PLMSearch; limitations (leakage, lack of statistics, bias towards well-sampled families)
- **Benchmarking:** structural classifications as ground truth; ROC, ROC$_n$, coverage vs. errors per query, E-value calibration; circularity, family-size bias and train–test leakage

## Further reading

### Background reading (open access)

- [Sequence homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence_homology)
- [Sequence alignment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence_alignment)
- [Needleman–Wunsch algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Needleman%E2%80%93Wunsch_algorithm)
- [Smith–Waterman algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith%E2%80%93Waterman_algorithm)
- [Substitution matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Substitution_matrix), [BLOSUM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BLOSUM), [PAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_accepted_mutation)
- [BLAST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BLAST_(biotechnology)), [FASTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FASTA)
- [NCBI: The Statistics of Sequence Similarity Scores](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/BLAST/tutorial/Altschul-1.html)
- [Hidden Markov model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidden_Markov_model), [Forward–backward algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward%E2%80%93backward_algorithm)
- [Additive smoothing ("pseudocounts")](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Additive_smoothing)
- [Multiple comparisons problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_comparisons_problem), [Family-wise error rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family-wise_error_rate)
- [Multiple sequence alignment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_sequence_alignment)
- [A tutorial on Burrows–Wheeler indexing methods](http://blog.thegrandlocus.com/2016/07/a-tutorial-on-burrows-wheeler-indexing-methods)

### Papers

Papers on the mandatory list above are not repeated here. ★ = mandatory in
earlier reading lists.

#### Reviews — start here

- @pearson2013 — an introduction to similarity searching, homology inference and statistics; the best single starting point.
- @eddy2004 — "What is a hidden Markov model?" (two pages).
- @eddy1998 — profile hidden Markov models.
- @lambert2003 — review of common sequence alignment methods.
- @bepler2021 — learning the protein language: evolution, structure and function.

#### Homology

- @reeck1987 — "homology" in proteins and nucleic acids: a terminology muddle and a way out of it.
- @doolittle1981 — similar amino acid sequences: chance or common ancestry?
- @rost1999 — the twilight zone of protein sequence alignments.
- @fitch1970 — distinguishing homologous from analogous proteins (orthology and paralogy defined).

#### Pairwise alignment and substitution matrices

- @bellman1954 — the theory of dynamic programming.
- @needleman1970 — global alignment by dynamic programming.
- @gotoh1982 — affine gap penalties in quadratic time.
- @myers1988 — optimal alignments in linear space.
- @dayhoff1978 — PAM matrices.
- @henikoff1992 — BLOSUM matrices.
- @altschul1991 — substitution matrices from an information-theoretic perspective.
- @eddy2004blosum — where did the BLOSUM62 matrix come from?

#### Heuristic search and statistics

- @pearson1988 — FASTA.
- @altschul1990 — the original BLAST.
- @karlin1990 — statistical significance of local alignment scores.
- @kent2002 — BLAT, for fast genome-scale alignment.
- @buchfink2021 — DIAMOND, BLAST-level sensitivity at much higher speed.
- @steinegger2018 — Linclust: clustering huge sequence sets in linear time.
- @barriohernandez2023 — clustering the AlphaFold database with Foldseek.
- @ferragina2000 — the FM-index.

#### Multiple sequence alignment and motifs

- @feng1987 — progressive alignment.
- @thompson1994 — ClustalW.
- @sievers2011 — Clustal Omega.
- @notredame2000 — T-Coffee (consistency).
- @edgar2004 — MUSCLE.
- @katoh2013 — MAFFT.
- @lawrence1993 — Gibbs sampling for subtle motifs.
- @bailey1994 — MEME (expectation maximisation).
- @schneider1990 — sequence logos.

#### Profiles and hidden Markov models

- @gribskov1987 — profile analysis.
- @park1998 — profile methods find three times as many remote homologues as pairwise methods.
- @krogh1994 — profile HMMs for protein families.
- @rabiner1989 — a tutorial on hidden Markov models.
- @eddy2008 — a probabilistic model of local alignment and significance estimation.
- @soding2005 — HMM–HMM comparison (HHsearch).
- ★ @remmert2012 — HHblits.
- @steinegger2019 — HH-suite3.

#### RNA homology search

- @eddy1994 — covariance models for RNA sequence analysis.
- @nawrocki2013 — Infernal 1.1: 100-fold faster RNA homology searches.
- @griffithsjones2003, @kalvari2021 — the Rfam database.
- @nussinov1980, @zuker1981 — RNA secondary structure by dynamic programming.
- @sankoff1985 — simultaneous folding and alignment.
- @rivas2017 — a statistical test for conserved RNA structure.
- @lowe1997 — tRNAscan-SE.

#### Alignment-free comparison

- @zielezinski2017 — review of alignment-free sequence comparison.
- @ondov2016 — Mash: genome distances with MinHash.
- @wood2014 — Kraken: metagenomic classification with $k$-mers.
- @jain2018ani — ANI and prokaryotic species boundaries.

#### Benchmarking

- @brenner1998 — assessing sequence comparison methods with structurally identified distant relationships.
- @lindahl2000 — identification of related proteins at family, superfamily and fold level.
- @gribskov1996 — ROC analysis of sequence matching.

#### Domains

- @sonnhammer1997 — Pfam: domain families from seed alignments.
- @mistry2021, @paysanlafosse2025 — Pfam today, including Pfam-N.
- @bileschi2022 — deep learning to annotate the protein universe (Pfam-N).
- @lau2024 — TED: the Encyclopedia of Domains in the AlphaFold database.

#### Protein language models

- @rives2021 — ESM-1b: biological structure and function emerge from unsupervised learning.
- @elnaggar2022 — ProtTrans.
- @lin2023 — ESM-2 and ESMFold.
- @hamamsy2024 — TM-Vec: remote homology from sequence embeddings.
- @hong2024 — dense retrieval for fast, sensitive homolog detection.
- @kaminski2023 — pLM-BLAST.
- @liu2024 — PLMSearch.
